summary: An 80-row rollout dataset analysed with a dependency-free Bun/TypeScript library, CLI, test suite, structured JSON, written analysis, and standalone HTML report. The finding: the candidate is not broadly slower — it is faster than control in 3 of 4 comparable region/device/cache strata, and the 90.9% worse aggregate is largely a traffic-mix artefact with the shape of Simpson's paradox, since the candidate arm carries 3.5x control's share of the slowest stratum. Standardising candidate stratum means onto the control mix moves 604.7 ms to 331.6 ms against a control 316.8 ms. The residual is real: one interaction, eu/mobile/cold, is genuinely regressed (798.3 ms n=4 to 1216.9 ms n=14, +52.4%), holds all four non-200 rows (504s, versus zero in control), and stays +44.9% when restricted to the 720-960 KB payload range both arms exercised, so larger candidate payloads do not explain it away. Payload is nonetheless only a marker rather than an identified mechanism: it explains about 36% of within-stratum variance, elapsed minute is a weaker competing correlate, and the relationship is not monotone. Because the arms ran in disjoint time windows (control 0-15, candidate 20-37) the variant is perfectly confounded with time, so the analysis reports association only and recommends holding the rollout for eu/mobile/cold while continuing elsewhere behind per-stratum guardrails, plus a randomised same-window A/B and latency-breakdown instrumentation as follow-ups.
known_issues: The dataset itself cannot support a causal claim: control and candidate ran in disjoint time windows, so the variant is fully confounded with time. This is a property of the supplied data, not of the analysis, and it is documented in the limitations section of every output.

The regressed stratum rests on 4 control rows against 14 candidate rows, and the payload-matched comparison on 4 control rows. The bootstrap interval reflects sampling variability only and is correspondingly wide; it does not account for the time-window confound.
p95 values at these sample sizes are close to the sample maximum and are labelled throughout as tail indicators rather than population estimates.
